analysis.one_liner: Bans cancer-linked and hormone-disrupting chemicals, including PFAS and formaldehyde, from cosmetics.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote and died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee at the end of the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal to sell cosmetics containing a list of chemicals tied to cancer, hormone disruption, or other harms: PFAS "forever chemicals," two phthalates, formaldehyde and related releasers, mercury, two little-used parabens, and two phenylenediamines. It was introduced in October 2021, sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who use makeup, nail products, hair straighteners, and other cosmetics every day. Exposure to formaldehyde from hair-straightening products and phthalates from fragranced products falls hardest on women and on salon and beauty workers who handle these products all day. The European Union already bans or restricts most of the chemicals on this list, so shoppers there get safer formulas; this bill would extend that protection to US shoppers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds these substances to the Food and Drug Administration's list of contaminants that make a cosmetic illegal to sell, so products containing them could no longer be marketed in the US [S3].
The ban would take effect January 1, 2025, giving companies time to reformulate [S3].

The banned list includes PFAS, phthalates, formaldehyde, mercury, and phenylenediamines, chemicals associated in the scientific literature with cancer, endocrine disruption, and allergic sensitization; under general knowledge, the EU has long restricted most of them, so compliant alternatives already exist on the market.

analysis.who_pays: Cosmetics and personal-care companies that would have to reformulate products, and the chemical suppliers that sell them these ingredients. Some of that cost could show up in prices, though firms already sell reformulated versions in the European market.

drawbacks.text: Reformulation is a real cost, and smaller indie beauty brands could feel it more than large multinationals, with some of the cost potentially passed to shoppers through prices.

The PFAS provision is written very broadly, covering any man-made chemical with even one fully fluorinated carbon atom, which critics could argue sweeps in trace contamination that poses little risk; a good-faith opponent would also note the bill bans by chemical list rather than by risk assessment and adds no new FDA testing resources [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case is strong: several listed chemicals, like formaldehyde in hair straighteners, are directly applied to skin and scalp, and salon workers face repeated exposure. The main costs are reformulation, which large firms already handle for the European market, and the broad PFAS definition, which could be tightened in committee. On balance the bill's benefits to consumers outweigh the compliance costs, though it is a narrow bill that bans chemicals without building out FDA's testing or enforcement capacity.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Jan Schakowsky introduced the Toxic-Free Beauty Act on October 8, 2021, joined by Representative Lizzie Fletcher [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and three days later to its Subcommittee on Health [S5].
The bill received no further action through January 3, 2023, when the 117th Congress ended, so it never came to a vote [S5].
The Congressional Research Service summarizes the bill as banning cosmetics that contain certain substances [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cosmetics and ingredient makers avoided a 2025 reformulation deadline, and US shoppers continued to buy products containing chemicals that are restricted in Europe.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Toxic-Free Beauty Act of 2021 in the House.

for.name: Rep. Lizzie Fletcher
for.what_they_did: Joined Schakowsky in introducing the bill.

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee markup or hearing; it sat at the subcommittee-referral stage for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Cosmetics and personal-care industry
against.what_they_did: Had an interest in avoiding a mandatory reformulation deadline for the listed chemicals; no formal opposition by the industry appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 initial supporters were House Democrats and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call reveals how the parties would have split; the record shows only that no action followed referral [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would force reformulation of products containing the banned chemicals by 2025, a compliance cost the industry avoided when the bill died. Because many large firms already sell reformulated versions in the EU, the cost is real but not prohibitive; their gain from the bill's death is shoppers' continued exposure.

Suppliers of phthalates, formaldehyde releasers, and PFAS ingredients would lose a product line if the ban took effect; their revenue depends on ingredients the bill deems unsafe for direct skin application.
